summary: Gives a history and description of the Internet Activities Board and its subsidiary organizations. It is a revision of RFC 1120 and informational only.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1160 describes how the Internet Activities Board (IAB) was organized in 1990. It explains the roles of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) and Internet Research Task Force (IRTF).

subtitle: A May 1990 account of the Internet Activities Board and its task forces.

tldr.problem: As Internet work grew, the community needed a description of the body coordinating its technical development and the groups doing that work.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recounts the IAB's origins, explains the IETF and IRTF, describes standards development and records the board's 1989–1990 agenda.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1160 is an Informational snapshot from May 1990 that obsoletes RFC 1120; it does not define a protocol standard.

today: RFC 1160 is an Informational memo published in May 1990 and obsoletes RFC 1120. It describes the IAB and its subsidiary groups as they were presented in 1990.

sections.title: How the Internet Activities Board Began
sections.content:
The memo traces the history from packet-switching research begun by DARPA in 1968 to the development of TCP/IP. As the research effort grew, an informal Internet Configuration Control Board was formed in 1979 to guide the protocols' technical development.

In 1983, the ICCB was reorganized around technical task forces and renamed the Internet Activities Board. The memo also describes the 1990 formation of the Federal Networking Council from the earlier FRICC.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB grew out of a committee created to guide Internet protocols. In 1983, that committee was reorganized into task forces and given the IAB name.

sections.title: The IAB's Role and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The IAB is described as the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering and management. Its functions include setting Internet standards, managing the RFC publication process, reviewing the IETF and IRTF, planning for the Internet's future and resolving technical issues that the task forces cannot handle.

The memo says IAB decisions are made public, mainly through the RFC series. It describes standards as progressing from Proposed Standard through Draft Standard to Standard after review, comment, implementation and testing.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB coordinated Internet technical work and the publication of RFCs. The memo says protocol standards passed through review, implementation and testing before reaching higher status.

sections.title: The Internet Engineering Task Force
sections.content:
The IETF coordinates Internet operation, management and development. In this memo, it is an open community organized into eight technical areas, with area directors and the IETF chair forming the Internet Engineering Steering Group.

Working Groups carry out much of the IETF's work. The memo reports more than 40 such groups and describes them as usually focused on a specific task.
sections.plainLanguage: The engineering task force brought together people working on the Internet. Topic areas and smaller teams organized that work.

sections.title: Research and the 1989–1990 Agenda
sections.content:
The IRTF promotes networking research and new technology. The memo says research and engineering can overlap, and describes Research Groups guided by the Internet Research Steering Group.

For 1989–1990, the IAB lists seven priorities: operational stability, user services, OSI coexistence, testbeds, security, Internet growth and higher speeds. The text discusses operational tools, directories, security guidance and preparation for more users, networks and faster links.
sections.plainLanguage: The research task force focused on study, while the engineering task force focused on technical work. The board's agenda covered stable operation, services, security, growth and speed.
